guides.title: Cartagena Day 4: Getse-Mania
guides.dek: Day 4 in Getsemani was such a whirlwind of color, music, and unexpected fun that we completely forgot to publish this post. Our original plan for Day 4 was simple: escape to the islands and spend the day surrounded by…
guides.body:
Day 4 in Getsemani was such a whirlwind of color, music, and unexpected fun that we completely forgot to publish this post. Our original plan for Day 4 was simple: escape to the islands and spend the day surrounded by turquoise water. Instead, Getsemaní cast its spell on us again, and we happily spent the day wandering deeper into its streets.

We eased into the day with a late lunch at the acclaimed La Cevichería, made famous in the U.S. by Anthony Bourdain and often praised for serving some of the freshest ceviche in Cartagena. After a string of underwhelming meals earlier in the trip, this one finally delivered: bright, clean flavors, generous portions, and fish so fresh it practically melted. There was no live music like at La Vitrola, but we did get front‑row seats to a video shoot happening outside Marzola Parrilla Argentina, whose lantern‑covered, mural‑filled façade made the perfect backdrop.

After a satisfying lunch, we stepped back into Cartagena’s past by visiting a pair of museums at the heart of the walled city. The Museo Histórico de Cartagena de Indias offered a stark look at the city’s experience under the Spanish Inquisition, sharing the stories of those accused of heresy in the New World. A short walk away, the Museo Casa del Oro traced the extractive legacy of colonial rule, when European powers stripped Colombia of much of its natural wealth.

We took a brief break at our hotel, then as dusk settled in, stepped back into Getsemani. Bar‑hopping in that neighborhood feels like slipping into a living mural, with music spilling from every doorway and color vibrating off the walls. Each bar has its own personality—rum‑soaked salsa dens, candlelit courtyards, and tiny family-run spots with tables spilling out into the sidewalks and alleys. We kicked things off at Casa Palenque, which offered a perfect view of the carnival performances at Plaza de La Trinidad. From there, we wandered from one lively street to the next, stopping along the way to sip a cocktail and take in the atmosphere. The whole neighborhood felt like one big open‑air party.

Hoping to keep the good vibes going, we broke up our bar‑hopping with dinner at Donjuán, another of Cartagena’s most-acclaimed restaurants. The dining room was undeniably beautiful—lush, elegant, and perfect for a slow tropical evening—but the food never matched the setting. Our fish‑and‑risotto dish arrived as a soft, shapeless mound resembling something off a kid’s menu. The risotto was so undercooked we could taste the starchy pearl, and the filet so overcooked it looked as if it had been rinsed with water before plating. The flavors echoed the presentation: flat, uneven, and ultimately forgettable. Perhaps we simply caught the kitchen on an off night.

Not wanting to end the night on that disappointing note, we slipped back into Getsemaní and let its energy pull us in again. By the time we made our way back to our hotel, we were exhausted but still tingling from the excitement. We’d experienced two versions of Cartagena—the walled city and Getsemaní’s vibrant maze—in a single, unforgettable day.

guides.title: Cartagena Day 6: Island Escapade
guides.dek: Our itinerary today had us visiting Cartagena’s local Barzuto Market followed by San Diego’s quiet elegance, but we have become weary of our routine: explore the city, shower, rinse and repeat. To break that cadence, we…
guides.body:
Our itinerary today had us visiting Cartagena’s local Barzuto Market followed by San Diego’s quiet elegance, but we have become weary of our routine: explore the city, shower, rinse and repeat. To break that cadence, we decided to go off to explore the islands, an excursion we had skipped earlier.

We chose the Blue Apple Resort, in part because it was highly rated and in part because one of the restaurants in Getsemani listed it in their “best things to do” in Cartagena list. The trip there involved a relaxing 20-minute speed boat ride leaving at 11:30 A.M., much less taxing than the 45 minute boat rides to Rosario, which typically leave at 7:30 A.M. Rather than have to rush out, we stocked up on provisions at the local market, then headed out to a day of rest and relaxation.

As the speed boat whisked us to the island of Baru, we caught some panoramic views of the neighborhoods we had visited earlier. Once we arrived we nestled into our beach side cabana for an uneventful day of rest and relaxation. The turquoise green waters were beautiful and warm. The air, tranquil and calm. The cabana, shaded underneath the hotel’s rustic chic garden, provided plenty of comfort. We could have hiked up and down the shoreline, but we didn’t. We just relaxed and took in the splendor.

After our boat ride back, we headed back to the hotel for a quick shower then went out for dinner at the nearby El Sombreron Ostreria. Colombians love shrimp cocktail, and they do it right. This is not your mother’s bland and boring boiled shrimp with cocktail sauce. No. Every bite of our cocktail was full of seasoned shrimp marinating in a delicious cocktail sauce, with brunoised onions, fresh herbs and lime. The cocktail is traditionally served with saltine crackers, which helps quiet your palate for the next, zesty bite. Ostrerias, which are very humble stands with plastic chairs, litter the streets near the murallas. We recommend trying one for a very tasty and inexpensive meal.

After dinner, we walked around the walled city, then headed back to the hotel. On the way, we remembered we had run out of beer and all the local supermarkets were already closed. Oh no! What to do?

Well, Cartagena has lots of mercados, the first floor of a building with twisting hallways that house all kinds of small shops, from barbers to cell phone repair shops. Some also house cafeterias, where Costenas gather to drink beer late at night. As luck would have it, the building right next to our cafeteria had just such a cafeteria, tucked way inside and towards the back of the mercardo. We heard the laughter from the street as we were approaching the hotel, cursing our fate. So we decided to stop by.

Costenas are warm inviting people, and the bar regulars were delighted to see us. We just wanted to buy a few roadies, but they pulled up a chair for us and started buying us rounds. The blue eyed bar tender was a former professional soccer player who, despite retiring from the sport, had retained his good looks. He shared with us his travel stories from his club team days: Brasil, Portugal and Norway. Our bar neighbor was an architect who restored old colonial houses and buildings. He showed us some of his projects, and even his YouTube channel. His work was gorgeous.

Day six was perfect; one of the best days we had during this visit. We tried escaping out tourist routine and ended up being welcomed by the locals. Check back tomorrow for our final day.

Today our Cartagena adventure took us on the Manga Waterfront Loop for some beautiful views of the city. We then dipped our toe into the local life just a bit, Unfortunately we woke up a bit late, so we had to face the heat as we walked around Manga:

Ease into the morning with breakfast of your choice, then walk or take a short Uber to Manga, a leafy residential peninsula with a breezy waterfront promenade.

Stroll the Paseo Peatonal de Manga, watching boats drift across the bay. Continue toward the Club de Pesca marina area for postcard‑worthy views of the Bocagrande skyline. Pause in Parque de la Marina, a shaded local park perfect for a quiet moment.

If you enjoy architecture, pass by Casa Roman, a striking historic mansion.

Return toward Old Town in the afternoon, stopping at Gelateria Paradiso for a refreshing treat. Spend the rest of the day revisiting favorite plazas or boutiques.

In the evening, enjoy rooftop drinks at Townhouse, followed by dinner at a restaurant you haven’t yet tried. Perhaps Celeste, a trendy and high-demand spot (reservations required 1 month in advance) in Centro or Carta Ajena Restaurante, a highly rated spot.

After having a light lunch at the Cerveceria Cartegena, we walked over to the Fuerte de San Sebastian del Pastilillo before seeing the Paseo Peatonal de Manga, the beautiful and elaborate Casa Roman, and Villa Susana, After Ubering back to the hotel for needed shower, we walked to Morena, an stunningly decorated Afro-Caribbean restaurant with delicious empanadas, then headed back to the Cerveceria to watch the Brasil v Columbia game. At halftime we hit Getsemani again to find more empanadas, and stumbled upon the aptly named Antojitos, a tiny mom and pop shop that’s definitely worth a visit for its delicious antojitos and great prices.

The day left us with this lovely blend of calm and connection. Walking along Manga’s waterfront, watching boats drift across the bay, and later wandering through Getsemani made the whole day feel expansive and intimate.

guides.title: Cartagena Day 3: Discovering the Lay of the Land
guides.dek: Our journey in Cartagena continued today with panoramic views, a tour of Getsemani and what should have been an unforgettable meal. By now we’ve learned to ignore the weather forecast, and we’re glad we did. Despite the…
guides.body:
Our journey in Cartagena continued today with panoramic views, a tour of Getsemani and what should have been an unforgettable meal. By now we’ve learned to ignore the weather forecast, and we’re glad we did. Despite the forecasted thunderstorm, the day turned out to be sunny and hot, providing us with the opportunity to discover some of what this city has to offer.

Here’s the itinerary we had planned for today.

Start your day at Época Espresso Bar, a Getsemaní favorite for specialty coffee and inventive breakfasts. Afterward, take a taxi to Convento de la Popa, perched high above the city. The monastery’s courtyard and chapel are serene, but the real highlight is the panoramic view stretching from the bay to the Caribbean Sea. Always take a taxi both ways — the hill is not walkable.

Back in the walled city, stop for lunch at Casa del Tunel Restaurante Bar, a breezy, open-air inner patio in Getsemaníat.

Afterwards, spend the afternoon exploring Las Bóvedas, a series of colonial vaults now filled with artisan shops selling mochilas, jewelry, hammocks, and handicrafts. From there, stroll past the elegant Teatro Adolfo Mejía, any remaining museums or through Parque del Centenario, a leafy space connecting Getsemaní and Old Town.

Dinner is at Carmen (reservations required), one of Cartagena’s most celebrated restaurants. Reservations are essential, and the experience is worth every bit of planning.

As with our other days here, though, we ended up making several adjustments. Instead of the Convento, we ended up taking an Uber to see the Castillo de San Felipe de Barajas, a landmark we had missed the day before. The fort offered a glimpse of the city’s history and panoramic views of the city. Plus the kids in us loved spelunking through the tunnels inside the fortified walls.

By now, we’ve also learned why the siesta was invented. Between noon and two, the sun breathes its fiery rays onto the city, casting it into the heat of a thousand furnaces. Only a Gringo tourist would be foolish enough to forge ahead. Determined not to become stereotypes, we retreated into the shelter of a the climate-controlled Mallplaza Cartegena. This mall, unlike the one from yesterday, was spacious and provided ample places to shop while escaping the furnace.

Afterwards we returned to the room for our second (of three) daily showers, then headed off to explore Getsemani. What a gem! Every wall is colorful or adorned with a mural or bomb graffiti. Overhead the neighbors hung paper flags, lanterns or umbrellas. There are craft stores and restaurants and cafes everywhere. It’s like Bat Man Alley and Rio’s Lapa, mashed together and spread out over dozens of city blocks. Compared to Tlaquepaque, which seemed designed for tourists, this neighborhood teemed with authenticity.

Lunch was at Casa del Tunnel, the restaurant we had wanted to visit yesterday. It serves a Caribbean menu in the courtyard of an old Spanish home decorated everywhere with folk art. With several large fig trees shading us, we enjoyed a mostly delicious meal. The ‘Leche de Tigre’ ceviche was flawless. The shrimp empanadas, however, had a greasy crust, as if they had been sitting for awhile before being refried. Overall, though, the restaurant provided a quaint and refreshing stop in the heart of a vibrantly Bohemian neighborhood.

After doing several laps around the narrow streets of Getsemani, we went back to our hotel for our third shower, then walked through old town heading off to our dinner reservation. Along the way, we saw a carnival troupe perform near the Plaza Santa Domingo. We then followed the murallas North to a corner of the old town we had not yet explored for our dinner at Carmen.

Perhaps because of our excellent day or perhaps because of the restaurants’ many great reviews, we arrived at Carmen with great expectations. We’re sorry to say that our experience did not live up to them. The ambiance was inviting enough: we dined in the courtyard beneath a white colonnade and thick trees. The food, however, was underwhelming. The dough on both our pasta and empanadas was too thick and doughy. The raviolis were visibly under cooked. Our fish, on the other hand, was overcooked and covered with a sandy farofa. Dry on dry. Honestly, given the restaurants many glowing reviews, maybe we caught it on an off night. But it was an expensive miss.

But let’s not let one bad experience spoil the bunch. Overall our day was both elevating and indulgent — like the city had given us its grandest vistas and then invited us to touch its craftsmanship with our own hands. Today was a satisfying blend of wonder and delight, the kind that comes from standing above a whole coastline one moment and then losing ourselves in colors, textures, and treasures the next.

Check back tomorrow for more updates!

guides.title: Cartagena Day 2: Cloudy Weather
guides.dek: “A good traveler has no fixed plans and is not intent on arriving.” That was the motto of our second day in Cartagena. We had planned to focus on the Old Town’s history and museums. Per our itinerary:
guides.body:
“A good traveler has no fixed plans and is not intent on arriving.” That was the motto of our second day in Cartagena. We had planned to focus on the Old Town’s history and museums. Per our itinerary:

Begin your morning with breakfast at Café Stepping Stone, a social‑impact café in Getsemaní known for excellent coffee and wholesome plates. From there, take a short taxi or a longer walk to Castillo San Felipe de Barajas, the imposing hilltop fortress that once guarded the city. Arrive early to avoid the heat and crowds, and explore its tunnels, battlements, and sweeping views.

Return to the walled city for a cluster of museums all within a few minutes of one another. Start at the Palace of the Inquisition on Plaza de Bolívar, then cross the square to the Gold Museum (Museo del Oro Zenú) for a compact but fascinating look at indigenous craftsmanship. Continue toward the waterfront to the Naval Museum of the Caribbean, which offers engaging exhibits on maritime history. If time allows, pass by the elegant Teatro Adolfo Mejía, a jewel of Cartagena’s cultural scene.

Lunch awaits at La Cevichería in Getsemaní, a lively, walk‑in‑only ceviche bar made famous by Anthony Bourdain.

Spend the afternoon strolling through Old Town’s boutiques, emerald shops, art galleries, and handicraft stores. As evening settles, relax in Plaza Santo Domingo, home to Botero’s famous sculpture “La Gorda Gertrudis.” Street performers, musicians, and warm lamplight make this plaza especially atmospheric.

Dinner tonight is at La Vitrola (reservations required), one of the city’s most iconic restaurants, known for its Cuban‑inspired ambiance and refined Caribbean dishes.

The weather forecasters, however, dashed our hopes for an outdoor excursion. Facing an 80% chance of mid-day rain, we put off our entire Day 2 itinerary and instead fast-forwarded our Day 7 plans, which involved shopping at the indoor Plaza Bocagrande Mall then exploring the Castillo Grande neighborhood, once the rains stopped. And so we headed out to the mall, confident that our revised itinerary would keep us dry.

It did, but not because the mall shielded us from the thunderstorm. Irony of ironies, it never did rain, so our cunning reshuffling turned out to be completely unnecessary. Doubly unnecessary because the mall itself had very few stores that were overpriced for our expectations, so our shopping ended quickly. The food court had plenty of options. The one we picked served us a Colombian fish stew whose recipe has been handed down for generations. Unfortunately, the fish in it had also seemingly been handed down for many generations.

The beaches just outside were as expected: underdeveloped with broken sidewalks and unkempt foreshore vegetation. The menacing clouds chased away the crowds but not the vendors, who politely but valiantly wanted to braid my hair.

Still, we had a lovely walk through Castillo Grande, the upscale and quiet neighborhood near the mall. There is a well paved walking trail on the Bahia the Cartegas side of this small peninsula. The other side has a very narrow, very local beach, the aptly name Playa Castillo Grande. At the very point of the peninsula sits the Fuerte Castillogrande, but don’t make the mistake we did. The fort sits inside a Naval Officer’s club, so it’s not open to visitors.

In the evening after washing the sweat off, we decided to explore the old city again, following the route we charted for our Day 1. Entering through the clock tower at Plaza de los Coches, we drifted through Calle Santo Domingo, Calle de la Factoria, and caught the breathtaking sunset at Las Murallas near the Baluarte de Santo Domingo for a golden‑hour panorama. We then wandered around the old city, ending up at the sweet‑filled Portal de los Dulces, where every cocada looked the same. Dinner was at La Vitrola. Highlights there included a live show by folk-Colombian musicians and an especially tasty yuca seafood empanada, whose seafood was from this century . The evening ended with a round or four of drinks at the very lively Mondo bar. We may have seen Colombian pop stars there but our pop-star knowledge begins in the Bay Area and ends in Puerto Rico.

A good traveled knows how to roll with the punches. And we did.

Check back tomorrow for more updates from our trip!

guides.title: Cartagena Day 1: Arrival
guides.dek: We’re excited to share with you that we’re taking our first trip to Latin America of the year, a special 2-week Valentine’s day trip to Cartagena and Playa del Carmen. We’ll be sharing some of what we discover each day in a…
guides.body:
We’re excited to share with you that we’re taking our first trip to Latin America of the year, a special 2-week Valentine’s day trip to Cartagena and Playa del Carmen. We’ll be sharing some of what we discover each day in a series of posts. Each one will be pretty short (we have some exploring to do), but hopefully what we learn on our trip will give you some tips and tricks for your own journey.

We arrived in Cartagena today after a seriously long trip, capped off by an even longer immigration line. Imagine going to Disney land in peak season without a priority pass, and you’ll pretty much understand what an ordeal it was. For us, it was two and a half hours standing shoulder to shoulder with our fellow travelers in a room with fan-controlled air conditioned. We think we saw someone bribe one of the attendants to get to the front of the line, and someone actually passed out while we were there!

But once we finally arrived at our hotel, our excitement energized us enough to start our exploration. Plus with rain in the forecast there’s no better time like the present to start exploring.

Here was the plan from our first-day itinerary:

Your Cartagena journey begins in the vibrant heart of Getsemaní, a neighborhood alive with color, music, and street art. After settling into your hotel, step outside and let the district introduce itself. Wander along Calle de la Sierpe, admire the murals splashed across the walls, and pause in Plaza de la Trinidad, where locals gather and the energy is unmistakably Caribbean.

For lunch, return to Getsemaní for a comforting, coastal meal at La Cocina de Pepina, a beloved spot serving traditional Colombian dishes with heart and heritage.

As the afternoon cools, walk toward the walled city. Enter through the clock tower at Plaza de los Coches, then drift through Calle Santo Domingo, Calle de la Factoria, and the sweet‑filled Portal de los Dulces. When the sun begins to sink, climb onto Las Murallas, the centuries‑old city walls, and follow them toward Baluarte de Santo Domingo for a golden‑hour panorama.

Finally follow the wall south to El Baluarte San Francisco Javier, a tapas bar with a terrace overlooking the water. You can dine there or end your evening back in Getsemaní with dinner at one of the local restaurants.

Because we unfortunately had to start our day a bit late, we had to skip a lot of the walking tour through the old city. We did make it to the Baluarte, however, ALMOST in time for the sunset. El Baluarte is a stunning cabana bar situated smack dab on top of the old walls, featuring live music, beautiful views of the ocean and old city, and delicious cocktails and drinks. It has a classically luxurious Cartagena ambiance mixed with spendid outdoor views. It was a spectacular introduction to the city. There was even a fireworks show just above the cabana that, we humbly believe, was staged to welcome us.

Later that evening we tried another excellent local bar, The Alquimista, whose mixologists create imaginative twists on classic cocktails. The Paloma with Tamarind and Mezcal was the best Paloma I’ve ever had in my life. The deconstructed Pina Coladas, made with Havana 7 (way better than Bacardi), were a tasty surprise, with a coconut candy taking the place of the traditional coconut milk foam.

Here is a visual journey of our first day. Check back tomorrow for more updates from our trip!

guides.title: Martha Medeiros in São Paulo: The Couture Poetry of Brazilian Lace
guides.dek: São Paulo rewards the traveler who looks closely. In Jardins, behind polished façades and beneath the shade of plane trees, the city’s fashion language reveals itself through texture: immaculate tailoring, sensual transparency…
guides.body:
São Paulo rewards the traveler who looks closely. In Jardins, behind polished façades and beneath the shade of plane trees, the city’s fashion language reveals itself through texture: immaculate tailoring, sensual transparency and details made slowly enough to hold a human story. At Martha Medeiros, Brazilian lace becomes the main event.

The Alagoas-born designer has built a luxury house around the delicacy and strength of handwork from Brazil’s Northeast. Her dresses, separates and bridal pieces do more than decorate the body. They turn centuries-old lace traditions into living, wearable architecture.

Begin on Rua Oscar Freire, then wander toward Rua Melo Alves, where São Paulo’s global polish meets a distinctly Brazilian appetite for craft and color. The Martha Medeiros boutique at Rua Melo Alves, 248 is a natural anchor for an afternoon devoted to design. The neighborhood invites comparison: international labels nearby, independent Brazilian voices around the corner, and cafés ready for the pause between fittings.

Pair the visit with our designer boutique walk through São Paulo’s Jardins district. Together, the stops make a persuasive case that the city’s most memorable luxury is not simply imported—it is imagined, cut and made in Brazil.

From Alagoas to a Brazilian Couture House

Martha Medeiros was born in Alagoas and began developing her eye for color, form and sewing early, inspired in part by her grandmother and the natural world around her. Before launching her namesake label in 2004, she led Maison M., a Maceió boutique that helped shape the city’s fashion scene from the 1980s onward.

Lace became the heart of the new house. The brand says it works with more than 450 women artisans from Brazil’s Northeast through Projeto Olhar do Sertão, an initiative of Instituto Martha Medeiros. Their handwork is combined with noble fabrics and rigorous pattern cutting, creating pieces that feel romantic without becoming nostalgic.

Renascença lace is one of the signatures worth examining at close range. According to the house, the entirely manual process begins with a detailed drawing fixed to a padded support. Using needles, cotton thread and narrow tape known as lacê, artisans build and connect the pattern one passage at a time. The result carries both delicacy and graphic structure.

Guipure brings a different character: more substantial, more architectural and especially beautiful when used to frame the waist, shoulder or hem. Medeiros often lets the lace define the silhouette, balancing transparency with precise construction so the effect is sensual yet composed.

Do not overlook the tailored jackets, crisp shirts, corseted tops and midi skirts. Current collections place lace beside jacquard, silk and sharply modeled forms. These pieces offer an easier route into the house than a full occasion gown and can be styled repeatedly across a sophisticated travel wardrobe.

Notice how the motif meets the seam, how the transparency is placed and how the garment moves rather than simply how it looks on the hanger. A lace dress should feel almost like a landscape around the body. Ask about the technique used in a piece and the time involved in its making; the story of the material is part of its value.

The brand currently lists the Melo Alves boutique at Rua Melo Alves, 248, Jardins, São Paulo, open Monday through Friday from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. and Saturday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Shopping Iguatemi and Palácio Tangará locations are also listed in São Paulo. Confirm hours directly before visiting, especially around holidays.

For a São Paulo afternoon, temper a lace blouse with high-waisted cream trousers, a lean blazer and sculptural gold earrings. A renascença midi skirt becomes modern with a fine knit, pointed flats and a structured bag. For dinner, let a single black or ivory lace dress carry the look; keep the shoes clean-lined and the hair polished rather than overly formal.

The most fashion-forward combination is lace against restraint. Avoid matching every romantic cue. A sharp jacket, minimal sandal or masculine watch gives the handwork space to feel contemporary. In the suitcase, one intricate piece can transform several familiar basics without demanding an entire occasion wardrobe.

Turn Brazilian lace, modern tailoring and the rhythm of Jardins into a destination wardrobe designed for the trip you are actually taking.

Martha Medeiros makes a compelling argument for slowness in one of Latin America’s fastest cities. Every tiny passage of lace holds precision, patience and the knowledge of its maker. Worn in São Paulo, it feels neither folkloric nor fragile. It feels assured: a couture language rooted in Brazil and ready for the world.

guides.dek: The art of the inverted diamond — sculptural jewelry that turns precious stones inside out, from a Jardins atelier with a rebellious streak.

The art of the inverted diamond — sculptural jewelry that turns precious stones inside out, from a Jardins atelier with a rebellious streak.

São Paulo rewards the eye that looks twice. Behind the polished façades of Jardins and the precise lines of Faria Lima, the city’s most compelling luxury often carries a sly disruption—a familiar form turned, tilted or exposed. Ara Vartanian’s jewelry belongs perfectly to this landscape: precious stones shown from unexpected angles, engineering made sensual, and glamour sharpened by a little rebellion.

The Brazilian jeweler is known for challenging conventional gemstone settings, creating pieces that feel timeless at first glance and quietly subversive at the second. For a fashion-focused day in São Paulo, his world offers an intimate way to encounter the city’s appetite for design, craft and confident individuality.

Begin in Jardins, where tree-lined streets gather Brazilian fashion, international houses and independent design. Ara Vartanian is available at NK Store on Rua Haddock Lobo 1592, while the official store directory also lists a boutique at Iguatemi São Paulo on Avenida Brigadeiro Faria Lima 2232. The brand’s São Paulo atelier welcomes visitors by appointment.

Make the jewelry stop part of our designer boutique walk through São Paulo’s Jardins district. The pleasure is in contrast: fluid Brazilian clothing beside stones set with architectural precision, then coffee or lunch nearby while the city’s creative language settles into focus.

Born in Beirut to an Armenian family, Ara Vartanian moved to Brazil when he was one. Gemstones were part of the family story: after settling in São Paulo, his father became a prominent supplier of diamonds and precious stones. Ara initially studied economics at Boston University and worked as a Nasdaq trader in New York before returning to Brazil in 2000 and entering the family business.

He began signing his own jewelry collections in 2002 and opened his namesake atelier in 2005. Classical knowledge became a foundation to push against. Rather than hiding a stone’s underside, Vartanian developed settings that reveal unexpected facets and make every angle part of the composition.

That appetite for creative exchange has extended to collaborations with contemporary artists Janaina Tschäpe and Ernesto Neto. In 2017, he worked with Kate Moss on a 27-piece collection. The house also credits Brazilian model Sabrina Gasperin as a longstanding muse and design collaborator, including on the bestselling Bone earring.

Vartanian’s signature gesture turns the conventional setting inside out, letting the pointed architecture of the stone become visible. The effect is tactile, modern and slightly dangerous.

A sculptural house favorite associated with Sabrina Gasperin, it brings organic form and polished metal close to the face.

Conceived around human connection, Link draws on Ara’s fascination with mechanics. Its bracelet closes with four inverted diamonds and can carry a private engraved message inside.

Look beyond diamonds to expressive tourmalines and colored stones. Ask where a stone originated and how its cut, setting and natural character shaped the finished design.

“The courage to expose a hidden facet, disturb a perfect symmetry.”

Treat Ara Vartanian jewelry as structure, not decoration. An inverted-diamond ring gives a cream trouser suit an intelligent edge; a single sculptural earring transforms a black column dress; a colored-stone pendant brings depth to an open white shirt. The most modern approach is restraint—one piece with enough visual tension to carry the look.

For São Paulo days, pair gold and dark stones with tobacco leather, crisp poplin and softly tailored linen. At night, let white diamonds flash against matte black or deep chocolate. Keep the neckline clean, the hair simple and the manicure polished but quiet. This jewelry is designed to be discovered from more than one angle.

A Different Angle on Brazilian Luxury

Ara Vartanian’s jewelry makes luxury feel curious again. The value lies not only in rarity, but in perspective: the courage to expose a hidden facet, disturb a perfect symmetry and allow precious materials to feel personal. In São Paulo, that balance of refinement and defiance looks entirely at home.

Jardins is São Paulo at its most elegant — leafy, polished, and effortlessly international. It’s where fashion houses, independent designers, art galleries, and quiet cafés create a neighborhood that feels made for slow, luxurious wandering. For the fashion lover, it’s a dream. Concept stores showcase emerging Brazilian designers alongside established icons, making Jardins the perfect place to discover pieces you won’t find anywhere else. From sculptural resort wear to finely tailored separates, the craftsmanship is unmistakable — bold, warm, and rooted in culture.

A curated walk through São Paulo’s most stylish neighborhood. Latin-American designers, luxury flagships, concept stores. Perfect for fashion lovers, collectors, and design-focused travelers. Boutique cafés and architectural gems along the way.

A perfect way to wander São Paulo’s Jardins district is to treat it like an elegant, slow‑moving promenade through the city’s most stylish streets.

Start your walk on Rua Oscar Freire, often compared to Rodeo Drive but with a distinctly Brazilian soul. The boutiques here are architectural statements: glass façades, sculptural interiors, warm lighting, and curated collections that celebrate both global and Latin-American design. It’s a street where every window feels like a mood board. Begin near Lenny Niemeyer, where refined swimwear sets the tone, then continue toward Carlos Miele, whose glamorous silhouettes anchor the street’s high‑fashion energy. Oscar Freire is leafy, walkable, and ideal for window‑shopping as you ease into the neighborhood’s rhythm.

From there, turn onto Alameda Lorena, a quieter, tree‑lined street with a more intimate boutique feel. Here you’ll find D’Arouche, offering contemporary tailoring with an edgy twist, and Surface to Air, a creative collective blending fashion and art. The shift from Oscar Freire’s luxury to Lorena’s indie sophistication gives the walk a natural flow.

Continue south to Alameda Franca, where Adriana Barra bursts with color, tropical prints, and bohemian glamour. Her boutique feels like stepping into a world of pattern and personality. Finally, head toward Rua Melo Alves to visit Alexandre Herchcovitch, one of Brazil’s most iconic avant‑garde designers.

This loop creates a seamless, romantic route through Jardins—equal parts fashion discovery, neighborhood charm, and leisurely exploration.

guides.title: Mountain Biking in São Paulo: Forested Highlands and Cross-Country Adventures
guides.dek: Embark on an exhilarating journey through the forested highlands of Brazil with mountain biking in São Paulo. From mist-covered trails to scenic ridgelines, this region blends nature, endurance, and adventure for cyclists…
guides.body:
Embark on an exhilarating journey through the forested highlands of Brazil with mountain biking in São Paulo. From mist-covered trails to scenic ridgelines, this region blends nature, endurance, and adventure for cyclists seeking Latin America’s most dynamic terrain.

Just beyond São Paulo’s urban sprawl lies a world of rolling green hills, misty forest reserves, and challenging singletrack. Mountain biking in São Paulo surprises many travelers — the region’s combination of Atlantic Forest (Mata Atlântica), rugged highland terrain, and well-developed trail networks makes it one of Brazil’s most rewarding MTB destinations.

Whether you’re chasing long endurance rides through protected forest or fast cross-country loops just outside the city, São Paulo offers a unique mix of accessibility and adventure.

🚴 Top Mountain Biking Routes & Tours

Located on São Paulo’s northern edge, Serra da Cantareira is one of the largest urban forests in the world and a mountain biking paradise. Expect shaded dirt climbs, forest singletrack, and sweeping viewpoints of the city below. Guided MTB tours range from half-day rides to endurance circuits for seasoned riders.

👉 Serra da Cantareira Biking Tours on TripAdvisor

Dominated by São Paulo’s highest peak, Pico do Jaraguá offers both technical ascents and thrilling descents through rugged terrain. Popular with local riders, this area has a mix of fire roads, singletrack, and forest paths. The summit rewards you with panoramic views stretching to the horizon.

3. São Paulo Countryside Endurance Rides

For riders looking to stretch their legs, several operators offer cross-country MTB tours through the rolling countryside outside the city. Think long gravel climbs, farm roads, and quiet rural scenery — perfect for intermediate to advanced cyclists seeking less technical but highly scenic routes.

Fly into São Paulo–Guarulhos International Airport (GRU), Brazil’s busiest hub and the main gateway for international travelers. Most MTB tours offer pick-up from central locations or can arrange transfers to parks and rural routes.

Browse curated offers for your next adventure.

São Paulo’s inland climate ranges from warm days to cool mornings in the highlands. Dress for layered comfort and endurance riding:

Lightweight or midweight MTB jersey Padded shorts or bibs for longer cross-country routes Light rain shell or windbreaker — showers can roll in unexpectedly Trail or SPD shoes with good traction for climbs and forest terrain Gloves with ventilation (the Atlantic Forest can be humid) Hydration pack or bottles — some areas have limited services

Best Season: May–September is São Paulo’s dry season with mild temps — perfect for long rides. October–April is warmer and wetter but brings lush greenery. Skill Level: Great mix. Cantareira and Pico do Jaraguá offer technical climbs and descents; countryside routes suit intermediate endurance riders. Insider Tip: Start rides early — morning mist in the Atlantic Forest gives the trails a magical feel, and you’ll beat midday heat and city traffic.

🇧🇷 Important Things to Know About Traveling to Brazil

Be prepared before visiting Brazil with key details on language, money, connectivity, and cultural etiquette to make your journey seamless and unforgettable.

Portuguese is Brazil’s official language and is spoken throughout the country. English is commonly understood in tourist destinations such as Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, and Bahia’s coastal resorts, but less so in smaller towns or rural regions. Learning a few basic phrases in Portuguese—like obrigado (thank you) or por favor (please)—will help you connect with locals and show respect for Brazil’s vibrant culture.

The official currency is the Brazilian Real (BRL), represented by the symbol “R$.” Banknotes are available in 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, and 100 reais, while coins range from 5 centavos to 1 real. Major credit and debit cards are accepted widely, though smaller establishments and street markets often prefer cash. ATMs are plentiful in urban centers—use those located inside banks or malls for safety.

Brazil offers some of the world’s most breathtaking travel experiences, from the beaches of Ipanema to the waterfalls of Iguaçu. While most visits are trouble-free, it’s wise to stay alert, especially in crowded areas or at night. Discover São Paulo’s Mercado Municipal—an iconic 1933 landmark blending neoclassical architecture, vibrant flavors, and authentic Brazilian culture.

Rising gracefully in São Paulo’s historic center, the Mercado Municipal de São Paulo — affectionately known as Mercadão — is more than a food market; it’s a cultural landmark. Opened in 1933, its neoclassical façade and vibrant stained-glass windows reflect a city shaped by waves of immigration and culinary exchange. For travelers weaving through Brazil’s bustling financial capital, this is the perfect place to slow down, taste the city’s heritage, and glimpse its everyday rhythm.

Inside, the market buzzes with energy: towers of tropical fruit, baskets of spices, wheels of artisan cheese, and the mouthwatering aroma of sizzling pastel de bacalhau. The Hocca Bar is a local institution — home of the legendary mortadella sandwich stacked thick enough to share. Order one, claim a counter seat, and watch the morning unfold as Paulistanos trade stories over cold beers and tourists snap photos beneath the soaring stained glass designed by Conrado Sorgenicht Filho.

guides.title: MAYDI in Buenos Aires: Argentina’s Quiet-Luxury Knitwear Story
guides.dek: Buenos Aires understands the elegance of a beautiful layer. Along Palermo’s tree-lined streets, tailored coats move past design studios and late-afternoon cafés; texture matters as much as silhouette. Into this cultivated…
guides.body:
Buenos Aires understands the elegance of a beautiful layer. Along Palermo’s tree-lined streets, tailored coats move past design studios and late-afternoon cafés; texture matters as much as silhouette. Into this cultivated rhythm comes MAYDI, María Abdala Zolezzi’s bespoke knitwear label built from Argentine fibers, handwork and an understated idea of luxury.

The clothes are quiet, but never anonymous. Fine merino, guanaco and llama give minimalist shapes depth; natural dyes carry the landscapes from which they came. Each piece is handmade to order, designed to live slowly and travel well.

A Buenos Aires Brand with a Franco-Argentine Lens

MAYDI was founded in 2014 when Abdala Zolezzi returned to Argentina after more than twelve years in Paris fashion. Her official biography traces a path through Totem, Showroom Robert Dodd, Sonia Rykiel, Isabel Marant and work connected to the Fédération Française de la Couture. Back in Buenos Aires, she asked what local resources could define a truly Argentine brand.

The answer was already embedded in the land: merino from Patagonia, llama from Jujuy, guanaco from Mendoza and a deep culture of knitting, crochet and loom work. MAYDI combines that material intelligence with the clean proportion of European luxury.

MAYDI says it holds no stock; every garment is handmade from beginning to end with local raw materials. The model turns waiting into part of the value of the piece. Craft is not accelerated out of sight—it remains visible in the finished knit.

The house uses natural and biodegradable animal and plant fibers. Its certified Wildlife Friendly merino and mohair come from Patagonian ranchers practicing regenerative grazing and coexistence with native species. Guanaco is sourced from a cooperative in Payunia, Mendoza, while llama and baby llama come from La Puna in Jujuy.

Patagonian merino: fine, soft wool made more meaningful by a wildlife-conscious sourcing story.

Guanaco: an exceptionally light, insulating special fiber, hand-extracted and processed through ancestral techniques.

Llama and baby llama: luminous fibers from Jujuy that bring warmth without heaviness.

Natural dyes: colors derived from materials including tara, palo amarillo, guayacán and cochineal, used to reconnect design with regional identity.

Hand-knit construction: crochet, traditional loom work and careful finishing that make each garment feel personal.

For Buenos Aires, layer a fine merino sweater over wide ivory trousers with a slim leather belt and a sculptural gold earring. In Patagonia, let a guanaco or llama knit soften technical outerwear and sturdy boots. For the flight, a long cardigan over a silk column creates polish without sacrificing comfort.

Keep the palette tonal—oat, tobacco, mineral gray, inky black—then add one note of natural dye. The luxury is in the hand of the fiber, so accessories should feel architectural rather than decorative.

guides.title: Buenos Aires Beauty: A Wonderful Walking Tour Through Palermo Soho and Recoleta
guides.dek: Buenos Aires blends European elegance with Latin American creativity, producing one of the most vibrant fashion scenes in the region. Independent designers, leather ateliers, and concept stores thrive here, especially in the…
guides.body:
Buenos Aires blends European elegance with Latin American creativity, producing one of the most vibrant fashion scenes in the region. Independent designers, leather ateliers, and concept stores thrive here, especially in the city’s most walkable creative districts. For boutique shopping, the top neighborhoods include Palermo Soho, known for its dense cluster of designers and concept stores; Palermo Hollywood, home to stylish boutiques and design studios; and Recoleta, where refined, upscale fashion meets classic Buenos Aires architecture. For a concentrated, highly walkable boutique experience, Palermo Soho offers the richest mix of contemporary Argentine design.

This article lays out a beautiful stroll through Buenos Aires’s most stylish neighborhoods. Perfect for fashion lovers, collectors, and design-focused travelers who enjoy getting to know the city’s neighborhoods and design culture.

Top Neighborhoods for Boutique Shopping in Buenos Aires

Palermo Soho — Independent designers, concept stores, leather goods, contemporary fashion

Palermo Hollywood — Trendy boutiques, design studios, minimalist fashion

Recoleta — Upscale boutiques, refined tailoring, luxury Argentine brands

Palermo Soho is one of the best neighborhoods to explore the city’s fashion on foot. This route is compact, stylish, and designed to showcase the best of Buenos Aires’ contemporary fashion scene in a single, effortless stroll.

Begin your walk at Plaza Armenia, one of Palermo Soho’s most recognizable landmarks and a perfect entry point into the neighborhood’s creative energy. From the plaza, head south along Nicaragua Street to reach Casa Rincón, a boutique known for its contemporary Argentine designers and beautifully curated accessories. Continue a few minutes toward Humawaca, a beloved brand specializing in modern leather goods and bold, architectural handbags that reflect Buenos Aires’ design-forward spirit.

As you move deeper into the neighborhood, follow the tree-lined streets toward Caro Criado, a boutique offering elegant womenswear with clean lines and a distinctly Argentine sensibility. A short walk away sits Calma Nena, a shop known for its playful, feminine silhouettes and colorful prints. The route flows naturally through Palermo Soho’s charming grid, where cobblestone streets and street art create a lively backdrop for boutique browsing.

Continue west toward Clara, a boutique that blends minimalist design with soft, neutral palettes, offering a refined counterpoint to the neighborhood’s bolder styles. Just a few minutes farther is Rapsodia, one of Argentina’s most iconic brands, known for bohemian-inspired fashion with intricate embroidery and global influences. End your walk at Paula Cahen D’Anvers, a classic Argentine label offering timeless pieces, tailored essentials, and a polished aesthetic that contrasts beautifully with the eclectic energy of Palermo Soho.

guides.body:
Buenos Aires is an extraordinary honeymoon destination because it blends European elegance with Latin American warmth, creating a city that feels both grand and intimate. Its architecture, leafy boulevards, passionate culture, and world‑class food scene make it a place where romance unfolds naturally. Couples can wander historic neighborhoods, linger over long dinners, dance tango under the stars, and escape to wine country or river towns—all within a single trip. It’s a city made for slow mornings, late nights, and unforgettable shared experiences.

Buenos Aires offers boutique hotels and stylish retreats perfect for newlyweds. CasaSur Palermo is a chic, modern option in the heart of Palermo Hollywood, with elegant suites and a rooftop pool ideal for relaxing between adventures. Legado Mítico in Palermo Soho offers a more intimate, design‑driven experience, with rooms inspired by Argentine cultural icons and a warm, romantic atmosphere. For classic luxury, Alvear Palace Hotel in Recoleta delivers old‑world glamour with marble interiors, impeccable service, and a stunning rooftop bar. Couples who prefer contemporary sophistication will love Fierro Hotel, known for spacious rooms and exceptional hospitality.

Buenos Aires is a city best explored at a leisurely pace. Start in Recoleta, visiting its historic cemetery, leafy plazas, and elegant cafés. Wander through Palermo Soho and Palermo Hollywood, where cobblestone streets, boutiques, and street art create a vibrant, youthful energy.

No honeymoon in Buenos Aires is complete without experiencing tango—whether watching a performance at Café de los Angelitos or taking a private lesson together. Art lovers can spend an afternoon at the MALBA or the Museo Nacional de Bellas Artes, while couples seeking a slower rhythm can enjoy a picnic in the rose gardens of Parque Tres de Febrero. Evenings are perfect for rooftop cocktails, wine tastings, or strolling through the romantic streets of San Telmo.

The city’s culinary scene is rich, diverse, and deeply romantic. For a special dinner, Don Julio offers world‑class Argentine steak in a warm, intimate setting. El Preferido de Palermo blends tradition and modernity with exceptional small plates and a charming pink façade. Casa Cavia is ideal for a honeymoon meal—set in a stunning mansion with a garden courtyard and refined, creative cuisine. For cocktails, Florería Atlántico delivers speakeasy magic, while Nicky Harrison offers a hidden, glamorous vibe behind a sushi bar.

Just outside the city, couples can escape to Tigre, where river canals, wooden docks, and quiet islands create a peaceful retreat. Colonia del Sacramento in Uruguay—reachable by ferry—offers cobblestone streets, seaside views, and a beautifully preserved historic quarter. Wine lovers can head to San Antonio de Areco or nearby estancias for horseback riding, traditional asados, and countryside serenity.

guides.title: The Quiet Luxury Weekend in Buenos Aires
guides.dek: Buenos Aires has a way of slowing your heartbeat the moment you arrive. The jacaranda-lined boulevards, the soft light over Recoleta, the marble cafés that feel untouched by time — it’s a city made for wandering, tasting, and…
guides.body:
Buenos Aires has a way of slowing your heartbeat the moment you arrive. The jacaranda-lined boulevards, the soft light over Recoleta, the marble cafés that feel untouched by time — it’s a city made for wandering, tasting, and falling in love with the small details.

A curated 72-hour escape for slow, elevated travel Boutique hotels in Recoleta & Palermo Tango shows, fine dining, rooftop views Perfect for a romantic, culture-infused weekend

Start your weekend in Recoleta, the neighborhood where old-world elegance meets modern calm. Imagine waking up in a boutique hotel suite with wrought-iron balconies, hearing nothing but the distant hum of the city and the soft clinking of breakfast china below. Step outside and walk through Recoleta Cemetery, not for the history alone, but for the architecture — quiet, ornate, almost cinematic.

As golden hour approaches, cross into Palermo. This is where the city breathes differently. Think leafy streets, design studios, wine bars with candlelit corners, and some of the best meals in Latin America. A long dinner at a chef’s table, followed by a slow walk back to your hotel, feels like its own kind of luxury.

Evenings in Buenos Aires are meant to linger. A tango performance in San Telmo — not the tourist kind, but the intimate, authentic show where every note feels alive — becomes one of those rare travel moments you remember for years. End the night on a rooftop terrace overlooking the lights of the city, the kind of setting that reminds you why you travel in the first place.

A quiet luxury weekend in Buenos Aires isn’t about rushing to see everything. It’s about intentionally savoring what the city naturally gives you: beauty, culture, warmth, and the gentle charm of simply being present.

guides.body:
There’s a quiet kind of magic that happens inside Buenos Aires’ cafés. Between marble tables, Belle Époque ceilings, and the soft hum of conversation, you feel like you’ve stepped into a slower era — one that prizes elegance, ritual, and people-watching over hurried schedules. Whether you’ve just landed on a LATAM flight or are unwinding at your Recoleta hotel, immersing yourself in café culture is a must for any luxury traveler.

Buenos Aires cafés are more than places to sip coffee; they’re living cultural institutions. Café Tortoni, with its stained glass and carved wood interiors, is the city’s most famous. Arrive early to avoid the lines, settle in with a medialuna (buttery croissant), and savor the atmosphere.

Elsewhere, in Recoleta, you’ll find elegant corner cafés that have hosted artists and intellectuals for over a century. Many of these historic gems are listed on TripAdvisor, making it easy to map out a self-guided café crawl or join a curated walking tour through Viator for insider stories and hidden favorites.

To make the most of your café explorations, stay in neighborhoods that put these cultural landmarks at your doorstep. Hotels.com has excellent options in Recoleta for travelers seeking old-world elegance, while Palermo offers contemporary boutique stays surrounded by leafy streets and modern design cafés.

After a morning of pastries and cortados, return to your room for a quick wardrobe change before your afternoon adventures — or continue your walk to nearby museums and tango theaters.

Café hopping in Buenos Aires works best on foot. The city is walkable and filled with architectural treasures between stops. Start at Café Tortoni, meander up Avenida de Mayo to Recoleta, and end your day in Palermo’s open-air cafés for sunset aperitifs.

For travelers who prefer structured experiences, book a Café & Architecture Tour on Viator. It’s an elegant way to dive into the stories behind these spaces without worrying about logistics. Pair the experience with a Welcome Pickups transfer to glide back to your hotel afterward, especially if you’re heading out for a tango show at night.

Buenos Aires rewards subtle elegance. Pack timeless pieces — tailored trousers, lightweight dresses, silk scarves — and elevate them with accessories from Olivela to fit seamlessly into the city’s aesthetic. Think “casual chic,” not athleisure.

If your café day falls on arrival or departure, treat yourself to a relaxing pause in a Priority Pass lounge before or after your flight. It’s the perfect complement to a day built around slow pleasures.

guides.body:
When night falls in Buenos Aires, the city transforms into a stage. Tango isn’t just danced here — it’s lived. And among countless performances across the city, three legendary venues set the standard for luxury, artistry, and atmosphere: Rojo Tango, Señor Tango, and Gala Tango. Whether you’re arriving via LATAM Airlines or settling into a Hotels.com boutique stay, these performances turn your trip into something unforgettable.

✨ Rojo Tango: Intimate Cabaret Glamour

Set within the iconic Faena Hotel, Rojo Tango is synonymous with exclusivity. Its intimate red-velvet setting channels vintage Parisian cabaret, while its choreography and live orchestra deliver a refined, sensual interpretation of traditional tango. The experience includes a gourmet dinner, elegant service, and world-class production values.

For VIP seating and priority entry, secure your spot through Ticketmaster. Pair your evening with a pre-show wine flight or rooftop cocktail in nearby Puerto Madero — easy to reach via a private Welcome Pickups transfer.

If Rojo Tango is cabaret, Señor Tango is Broadway. Known for its theatrical scale — live horses, sweeping stages, and dramatic lighting — this show immerses you in a tango opera that’s larger than life. While purists may prefer smaller venues, travelers seeking an unforgettable spectacle love its emotional power.

Arrive dressed elegantly, ideally wearing a signature Olivela accessory that elevates your look. VIP seats on Ticketmaster often include dinner, premium drinks, and chauffeured options. Book early during peak season.

🏛 Gala Tango: Classic Elegance in a French Mansion

For many luxury travelers, Gala Tango strikes the perfect balance between Rojo’s intimacy and Señor Tango’s grandeur. Housed in a beautifully restored mansion, the experience begins the moment you step through its gilded doors. The choreography is traditional, the music impeccable, and the setting impossibly romantic.

guides.body:
Do you want to get around Guadalajara like a local? Then it’s time to get acquainted with the city’s metro system and bike paths. The city’s public transportation and rideable/walkable routes provide travelers with diverse and efficient ways to get out of the car and see places that are not yet on the “map.” Get a little turned around? That’s part of the journey.

This article covers our favorite way to explore Guadalajara: without a car or taxi.

Guadalajara’s Sistema de Tren Eléctrico Urbano (SITEUR—we’ll just call it the metro—is a modern light‑rail system with four lines and 57 stations. A single ride costs 9.50 pesos (about $0.55 USD), payable with cash or the rechargeable Tarjeta de Movilidad Integrada, which can also be topped up at OXXO convenience stores. That makes it one of the easiest and most affordable ways to get around.

The metro operates daily from 5:00 a.m. to 11:00 p.m., connecting key districts like Zapopan, Tlaquepaque, and downtown Guadalajara. Line 1 (blue) runs north–south, Line 2 (green) east–west, while Line 3 (red) links Zapopan to Tlaquepaque, which features a beautiful station just steps away from the historic center. A new Line 4 is under construction to extend service further south.

For planning, the official SITEUR website provides updated schedules, fares, and service notices: SITEUR Official Site. You can also download a clear system map from Mapa Metro Guadalajara or consult guides like MetroEasy Guadalajara. You can also use Google Maps to easily plan your metro journey.

Timing is everything: Avoid rush hours (7–9 a.m. and 5–7 p.m.) as train tend to get very crowded (though not quite as crowded as in Mexico City).

Stay Safe: The system is generally safe: you’ll see a lot of locals using their phones. Still, it’s always a good idea to keep belongings secure.

Cash is King: Keep small change handy if paying cash at turnstiles.

Buy a single ticket (9.50 pesos) at station booths with cash.

For convenience, purchase a Tarjeta de Movilidad Integrada (rechargeable smart card) that also works on buses and can be topped up at OXXO convenience stores.

Tap your card on the reader or insert your paper ticket at the turnstile.

Follow color‑coded line signs (blue, green, red) to find your train.

Trains run every few minutes from 5:00 a.m. to 11:00 p.m..

To transfer, follow posted arrows and maps—symbols make navigation easier.

With affordable fares, frequent trains, and easy‑to‑read maps, Guadalajara’s metro is a reliable way to reach attractions like the historic center, Tlaquepaque’s artisan markets, and Zapopan’s cultural district.

Guadalajara is steadily building its cycling infrastructure, with more than 150 km of protected bike lanes connecting historic neighborhoods, parks, and modern districts. Riding a bike here requires some experience with urban biking, but it is also one of the best ways to experience the city’s vibrant streets and plazas.

Over the past decade, the city has expanded its cycling infrastructure along major avenues such as Avenida Vallarta, Calzada Federalismo, and the Ruta del Río, making them safer corridors for commuters and leisure riders. The Centro Histórico is increasingly bike‑friendly, with lanes linking landmarks like the Cathedral and Plaza de Armas. To the west, Zapopan offers wide boulevards and access to cultural sites, while Providencia and Chapalita feature leafy residential streets with marked paths ideal for casual rides.

Cyclists also enjoy routes to green spaces such as Parque Los Colomos and Parque José Clemente Orozco, both accessible via bike lanes and offering scenic escapes from traffic. Weekend riders often take advantage of loops around Lake Chapala or suburban trails, combining urban convenience with natural beauty.

Guadalajara also hosts the weekly *Vía RecreActiva* events, closing major avenues every Sunday from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m. for cyclists, runners, and families. Streets like Avenida Vallarta, Avenida Juárez, and Chapultepec transform into corridors filled with bikes, music, and community activities, offering a joyful, car‑free urban experience.

Safety: Depending on your experience level, we recommend sticking to dedicated bike lanes or biking Sundays on the closed-off avenues. Even if you’re an experienced urban cycler, remember that many Latin American drivers are fans on Formula 1.

By choosing public transit, walking, or biking, you’ll not only save money—you’ll experience the city like a local. From art galleries to museums, getting around without a taxi opens up a more authentic, sustainable way to explore Guadalajara.

Be prepared before visiting Mexico with key insights on language, money, connectivity, and cultural etiquette.

Spanish is Mexico’s official language, though English is widely spoken in major tourist areas, resorts, and international hubs like Cancún, Los Cabos, and Mexico City. In rural regions and local markets, Spanish (and sometimes Indigenous languages such as Nahuatl or Maya) are more common. Learning a few essential phrases—por favor, gracias, buenos días—goes a long way in showing respect and connection.

The official currency is the Mexican Peso (MXN), typically shown with the “$” symbol. Banknotes come in denominations of 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, and 1 000 pesos, while coins range from 1 to 20 pesos. Most major cards are accepted, but some small restaurants, markets, and taxis prefer cash. Always confirm whether prices are listed in pesos or U.S. dollars to avoid confusion.

Mexico is generally welcoming and safe for visitors who stay aware and informed. Tourist zones like Riviera Maya, Puerto Vallarta, Oaxaca, and Mérida are known for their hospitality and police presence. Use registered taxis or rideshare apps, avoid displaying valuables, and check local travel advisories before venturing into remote areas. Trust your instincts—Mexican warmth and kindness shine brightest when you travel mindfully.

ATMs (cajeros automáticos) are widely available in cities, airports, and shopping centers, dispensing pesos directly. Use ATMs inside banks for added security. Visa, Mastercard, and AMEX are broadly accepted, though smaller hotels and cafés may charge a card fee. Q: Is it better to stay in Playa del Carmen or Tulum? A: Playa del Carmen is ideal if you want walkable dining, shopping, and nightlife with a more urban‑beach feel. Q: When is the best time to visit the Riviera Maya in 2026? A: The best months are typically from late November to April, when the weather is drier and less humid. Summer can be beautiful but warmer, with a higher chance of rain and sargassum on some beaches.

Q: Are boutique hotels in Tulum and Playa del Carmen family‑friendly? A: Some are, but many of the most stylish boutique properties are designed with couples and adults in mind. Always check age policies—certain hotels lean into honeymoon, wellness, or adults‑only experiences.

Be prepared before visiting Mexico with key insights on language, money, connectivity, and cultural etiquette.

Spanish is Mexico’s official language, though English is widely spoken in major tourist areas, resorts, and international hubs like Cancún, Los Cabos, and Mexico City. In rural regions and local markets, Spanish (and sometimes Indigenous languages such as Nahuatl or Maya) are more common. Learning a few essential phrases—por favor, gracias, buenos días—goes a long way in showing respect and connection.

The official currency is the Mexican Peso (MXN), typically shown with the “$” symbol. Banknotes come in denominations of 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, and 1 000 pesos, while coins range from 1 to 20 pesos. Most major cards are accepted, but some small restaurants, markets, and taxis prefer cash. Always confirm whether prices are listed in pesos or U.S. dollars to avoid confusion.

Mexico is generally welcoming and safe for visitors who stay aware and informed. Tourist zones like Riviera Maya, Puerto Vallarta, Oaxaca, and Mérida are known for their hospitality and police presence. Use registered taxis or rideshare apps, avoid displaying valuables, and check local travel advisories before venturing into remote areas. Trust your instincts—Mexican warmth and kindness shine brightest when you travel mindfully.

ATMs (cajeros automáticos) are widely available in cities, airports, and shopping centers, dispensing pesos directly. Use ATMs inside banks for added security. Visa, Mastercard, and AMEX are broadly accepted, though smaller hotels and cafés may charge a card fee. Tipping (10–15 %) is customary in restaurants, and cash tips are appreciated for hotel staff, guides, and drivers.

Mexico uses Type A and Type B power sockets, the same as the United States and Canada, with a standard voltage of 127 V and frequency of 60 Hz. Visitors from North America typically won’t need an adapter, while travelers from Europe, Asia, or South America should bring a universal plug and possibly a voltage converter for hair tools or appliances.

Wander toward Parque Fundadores to see the Portal Maya sculpture and catch live performances.

Midday — Playa Fundadores / Main Beach

Playa del Carmen has a way of pulling you in with its mix of Caribbean beauty, walkable charm, and a rhythm that feels both relaxed and effortlessly stylish. It’s a place where you can spend mornings swimming in turquoise water, afternoons wandering shaded streets lined with boutiques and cafés, and evenings savoring fresh seafood under the stars. For honeymooners, families, or solo travelers, Playa offers that sweet spot between beach escape and cultural immersion—close to world‑class nature, Mayan history, and some of the best dining in the Riviera Maya.

We’re preparing our own trip to Playa del Carmen, so we wanted to share our research with you.

Most visitors fly into Cancún International Airport (CUN), one of the busiest hubs in the Caribbean. From there, Playa del Carmen is about a 45–60 minute drive south along Highway 307. Transportation options are plentiful:

Private transfers: The most comfortable and efficient option, especially if you’re carrying luggage or arriving late.

ADO bus: Affordable, air‑conditioned, and reliable, with direct routes from the airport to Playa’s downtown terminal.

Rental cars: Ideal if you plan to explore cenotes, Tulum, or the surrounding region at your own pace.

Taxis: Available at the airport, though typically more expensive than pre‑booked transfers.

Once in Playa, the town is extremely walkable, especially around the beach and Fifth Avenue.

Playa del Carmen offers a wide range of accommodations, from boutique hideaways to modern suites steps from the beach.

Playa del Carmen’s dining scene is one of the most diverse in the Riviera Maya, blending Mexican flavors with international influences.

Alux Restaurant: A dramatic dining experience set inside a natural cave. The atmosphere alone makes it worth a visit.

La Cueva del Chango: A beloved breakfast and lunch spot surrounded by tropical greenery. Try the chilaquiles or fresh juices.

Trattoria del Centro: Excellent handmade pasta and Italian classics in a cozy, romantic setting.

Los Aguachiles: A casual favorite for seafood lovers—ceviches, tostadas, and shrimp tacos with bold Yucatán flavors.

Oh Lala!: An intimate fine‑dining restaurant with a small menu focused on quality ingredients and personalized service.

El Fogón: A must‑visit for authentic tacos al pastor and traditional Mexican dishes. Affordable, lively, and delicious.

While Playa is best known for its beaches, it also offers cultural experiences worth exploring.

Frida Kahlo Museum Playa del Carmen: A modern, interactive museum celebrating the life and work of one of Mexico’s most iconic artists.

3D Museum of Wonders: A fun, immersive museum featuring optical‑illusion art—great for photos and a break from the sun.

Nuestra Señora del Carmen Catholic Church: A small but beautiful whitewashed church near Parque Fundadores, often hosting weddings and local celebrations.

Parque Fundadores: Home to the iconic Portal Maya sculpture, this beachfront park is a cultural hub with performances, music, and artisan vendors.

Playa del Carmen is perfectly positioned for adventure, nature, and history.

Snorkeling, paddleboarding, and catamaran cruises are all popular. The nearby reef offers excellent underwater life, especially around Puerto Morelos.

The region is dotted with freshwater sinkholes perfect for swimming and exploring. Favorites near Playa include Cenote Azul, Cenote Cristalino, and Jardín del Eden.

Tulum: Oceanfront ruins with breathtaking views.

Cobá: A jungle‑covered archaeological site where you can bike between structures.

Chichén Itzá: One of the New Seven Wonders of the World, ideal for a full‑day excursion.

A short ferry ride from Playa, Cozumel offers world‑class diving, beaches, and a charming town center.

Xcaret, Xplor, and Xel‑Há offer a mix of nature, adventure, and cultural shows—great for families or couples.

Playa del Carmen blends the best of the Yucatán Peninsula into one compact, easy‑to‑navigate destination. The beaches are wide and inviting, the water warm year‑round, and the town itself has a cosmopolitan feel thanks to its mix of Mexican, European, and international influences. Fifth Avenue (La Quinta Avenida) is the beating heart of the city, offering endless restaurants, bars, artisan shops, and galleries. Beyond the town, you’re minutes from cenotes, jungle adventures, Mayan ruins, and protected natural reserves. It’s a destination where you can be as active or as relaxed as you want.

🇲🇽 Important Things to Know About Traveling to Mexico

Be prepared before visiting Mexico with key insights on language, money, connectivity, and cultural etiquette.

Spanish is Mexico’s official language, though English is widely spoken in major tourist areas, resorts, and international hubs like Cancún, Los Cabos, and Mexico City. In rural regions and local markets, Spanish (and sometimes Indigenous languages such as Nahuatl or Maya) are more common. Learning a few essential phrases—por favor, gracias, buenos días—goes a long way in showing respect and connection.

The official currency is the Mexican Peso (MXN), typically shown with the “$” symbol. Banknotes come in denominations of 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, and 1 000 pesos, while coins range from 1 to 20 pesos. Most major cards are accepted, but some small restaurants, markets, and taxis prefer cash. Always confirm whether prices are listed in pesos or U.S. dollars to avoid confusion.

Mexico is generally welcoming and safe for visitors who stay aware and informed. Tourist zones like Riviera Maya, Puerto Vallarta, Oaxaca, and Mérida are known for their hospitality and police presence. Use registered taxis or rideshare apps, avoid displaying valuables, and check local travel advisories before venturing into remote areas. Trust your instincts—Mexican warmth and kindness shine brightest when you travel mindfully.

ATMs (cajeros automáticos) are widely available in cities, airports, and shopping centers, dispensing pesos directly. Use ATMs inside banks for added security. Visa, Mastercard, and AMEX are broadly accepted, though smaller hotels and cafés may charge a card fee. Tipping (10–15 %) is customary in restaurants, and cash tips are appreciated for hotel staff, guides, and drivers.

Mexico uses Type A and Type B power sockets, the same as the United States and Canada, with a standard voltage of 127 V and frequency of 60 Hz. Visitors from North America typically won’t need an adapter, while travelers from Europe, Asia, or South America should bring a universal plug and possibly a voltage converter for hair tools or appliances.

Wi-Fi is accessible in most hotels, cafés, and airports, though speeds vary outside urban areas. Major telecom providers—Telcel, AT&T México, and Movistar—offer strong 4G coverage across cities and resorts. For longer stays, consider buying a local SIM card or using an eSIM like Yesim to stay connected while exploring Mexico’s beaches, ruins, and pueblos mágicos.

Citizens of the U.S., Canada, the U.K., and most EU countries can enter Mexico visa-free for tourism up to 180 days. Travelers must complete an immigration form (FMM) upon arrival—some airlines include it in ticketing. Always check that your passport is valid for at least 6 months beyond your travel dates. Keep your FMM card safe; you’ll need it when departing the country.
